paragraphs: This paper develops a physical neural network chip for an image-processing step used in phase-based vision. The authors describe its design, fabrication, and testing in analog CMOS circuitry. Its central operation resembles Gabor filtering, which transforms an image into a representation that carries local phase information.

The important feature is that the filter output has two parts: real and imaginary. Together, these define a phase value at each pixel. The chip produces both parts directly from an input image, making the information needed for phase-based processing available through its hardware outputs.

The abstract connects this representation to estimating differences between stereo images, controlling the alignment of binocular views, and analyzing image motion. These are motivations for the filtering hardware rather than separate reported application results. The contribution is a fabricated and tested prototype that implements the relevant image transformation, providing a concrete hardware building block for vision algorithms that use phase.
neurips-1997-an-analog-vlsi-neural-netwo.tldr: A fabricated analog neural-network chip produces the two image-filter outputs needed to compute local phase for machine vision.

paragraphs: This paper builds an analog hardware model of how repeated biological segments coordinate rhythmic activity. The implemented system contains eleven pattern-generating circuits arranged in a chain. Each circuit communicates through synaptic connections only with its immediate neighbors, so coordination is studied through local interactions between adjacent oscillators.

Each pattern generator contains two silicon implementations of Morris-Lecar neurons. The neurons inhibit one another, creating a small reciprocal network whose oscillation mechanisms the authors examine. This two-cell circuit supplies the repeating unit for the larger chain, connecting the behavior of an individual rhythm generator to the behavior of the coordinated system.

The authors test the hardware and explore how its behavior changes with isotropic or anisotropic coupling and with frequency gradients along the chain. These variations examine the roles of directional coupling and differences in oscillator frequency. The work therefore provides a physical platform for investigating how local neural connections can organize rhythms across multiple segments, with explicit control over several features of those connections.
neurips-1997-analog-vlsi-model-of-inters.tldr: An eleven-stage analog neural circuit models rhythmic coordination through interactions between neighboring oscillators.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a practical problem in associative memory: retrieving a stored pattern from an imperfect or mixed cue. The Willshaw model offers high theoretical information capacity for sparse patterns, but interference between stored memories creates substantial retrieval noise in finite systems. This weakens the practical value of its asymptotic capacity.

The authors introduce crosswise bidirectional retrieval, an iterative method that uses retrieval in both directions. They investigate its capacity limit, analyze the first retrieval step, and compare its performance experimentally with the Willshaw model. The reported improvement concerns the retrieval procedure, making stored associations more usable despite interference.

The experiments also examine cues formed by superimposing patterns, rather than only corrupting a pattern with random noise. The method can separate patterns from these mixed addresses even at high memory load. That result matters for the proposed uses in information retrieval and models of reciprocal cortical pathways, where a useful memory must handle structured mixtures as well as noisy inputs.
neurips-1997-bidirectional-retrieval-fro.tldr: An iterative bidirectional retrieval method improves Willshaw associative memory and can separate superimposed patterns at high memory load.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to combine classifiers produced by different learning algorithms. Such classifiers may represent data differently or search for solutions in different ways. The authors focus on using this diversity, extending beyond the familiar strategy of repeatedly training one algorithm on altered versions of the same dataset.

Their method combines stacking with correspondence analysis to represent relationships between training examples and the predictions made about them. The collection of classifier outputs becomes information for another stage of learning. A nearest-neighbor method then classifies new examples within the representation constructed from those relationships.

This approach makes the pattern of agreement and disagreement among models part of the classification process, rather than reducing their predictions immediately to a prescribed vote. Across the evaluated datasets, the algorithm consistently matches or exceeds the performance of other combination techniques. The stated finding supports learning how heterogeneous classifiers relate to examples as a useful basis for combining their predictions.
neurips-1997-combining-classifiers-using.tldr: The method combines diverse classifiers by learning a representation of their predictions and applying nearest-neighbor classification within it.

paragraphs: This paper develops a face detector around autoassociative neural networks, which reconstruct their inputs through a reduced representation. Detection depends on how far an image window lies from the learned set of faces. A threshold on reconstruction-based distance controls how readily the system accepts a window as a face.

The supplied evidence identifies two difficulties: the learned representation may also reconstruct non-faces, and training may settle near a linear solution. The authors use non-face counterexamples and constraints to shape a nonlinear representation. Rather than reconstructing these counterexamples unchanged, the network is trained toward an approximation of their projection onto the face set.

The paper then compares ensembles, conditional ensembles, and conditional mixtures of networks to improve coverage of face orientations and reduce false alarms. It reports that the conditional mixture achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark face databases. The approach joins a constrained reconstruction model with a choice of how multiple networks contribute to the final detection.
neurips-1997-ensemble-and-modular-approa.tldr: Constrained reconstruction networks combined in a conditional mixture achieve strong benchmark face detection across orientations.

paragraphs: This paper improves a Bayesian approach to neural-network learning that approximates uncertainty over the network's weights. The approach fits a parameterized distribution to the posterior by minimizing a Kullback-Leibler divergence. Its aim is to represent a range of plausible weight settings within a manageable mathematical form.

An earlier deterministic version required a Gaussian approximation with diagonal covariance. That restriction prevents it from representing posterior correlations between different parameters: uncertainty about one weight cannot be linked to uncertainty about another. The authors extend the method to full-covariance Gaussian distributions while keeping the computation tractable, allowing these relationships to enter the approximation.

They also incorporate hyperparameters into the framework and derive a simple procedure for re-estimating them. Initial benchmark results are described as encouraging. The main contribution is the expanded approximation machinery: it accommodates richer relationships among weights and supports hyperparameter estimation without abandoning a tractable deterministic learning approach. The empirical evidence is explicitly presented as preliminary.
neurips-1997-ensemble-learning-for-multi.tldr: Bayesian ensemble learning is extended to capture correlations between neural-network weights while remaining computationally tractable.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a probability model for data whose dependence relationships are sparse and can change. Its central idea is a mixture of trees: multiple tree structures participate in the model, so one fixed pattern of dependencies does not have to explain all the data. Dependency structure itself becomes something to infer.

The authors develop efficient learning algorithms by combining expectation-maximization with a minimum spanning tree algorithm. These two ingredients address the mixture and structural aspects of the problem together. The resulting framework learns both how the mixture is organized and which tree-shaped dependency structures it uses.

The algorithms support maximum-likelihood estimation and maximum a posteriori estimation, which incorporates prior preferences into fitting. The paper covers several priors, including Dirichlet and minimum-description-length priors. Its contribution is thus both representational and computational: it provides a way to express changing sparse relationships and a family of efficient procedures for estimating them under different statistical criteria.
neurips-1997-estimating-dependency-struc.tldr: Mixtures of trees model changing sparse dependencies and can be learned efficiently using EM and minimum spanning tree algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper establishes a mathematical connection between regularization networks and support vector machines. It relates the operators used to specify regularization in one framework to the kernels used in the other. The connection explains how these apparently different mathematical choices can encode equivalent regularization properties.

The central result concerns Green's functions associated with regularization operators. The authors prove that these functions can serve as suitable support vector kernels. This makes the relationship constructive: a regularization operator supplies a route to a corresponding kernel, with a stated equivalence in the regularization it imposes.

A further result expands the available kernel choices to a large family of radial basis functions, specifically conditionally positive definite functions. The significance is theoretical rather than an application benchmark: the paper gives a principled link between choosing regularization and choosing a kernel. That link helps interpret kernels through their regularization properties and identifies additional functions that can be used in support vector methods.
neurips-1997-from-regularization-operato.tldr: The paper proves that Green's functions of regularization operators yield support vector kernels with equivalent regularization properties.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to choose an online learning rule when the objective is improvement over the entire learning process. It studies a soft committee machine within a statistical-mechanics framework. The quantity being optimized is generalization error, which concerns the model's performance beyond the examples used to learn.

Earlier locally optimal rules considered how quickly generalization error decreases at the current stage. The authors instead maximize its total reduction across the learning process. This changes the optimization problem from choosing the best immediate improvement to choosing a rule according to the consequences of the full learning trajectory.

The resulting rule can significantly outperform the locally optimal rule in the setting studied. The finding shows why optimizing an instantaneous rate of progress need not optimize learning as a whole. The contribution is a method for deriving a globally optimal rule for the specified model and framework, together with a comparison demonstrating the value of that broader objective.
neurips-1997-globally-optimal-on-line-le.tldr: Optimizing improvement across the full learning process can outperform an online rule that maximizes only immediate progress.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning to rank from judgments that one item should appear before another. Its approach separates the task into two stages. First, a learner constructs a preference function for pairs of items. Then an ordering procedure arranges new items to agree with as many learned preferences as possible.

Turning pairwise preferences into the best overall ordering is itself difficult. The authors prove that finding the ordering with maximum agreement is NP-complete, even under restrictive assumptions. They therefore provide a simple greedy algorithm with an approximation guarantee, making the second stage usable without requiring an exact solution.

The paper also develops an online method based on Hedge for learning a linear combination of ranking experts. It combines this learning method with the ordering algorithm in a web-search application, where experts are domain-specific query-expansion strategies. Reported experiments support the approach. The contribution joins preference learning, approximate ordering, and adaptive expert combination into one ranking workflow.
neurips-1997-learning-to-order-things-08.tldr: The paper learns pairwise preferences and combines ranking experts, then efficiently approximates an ordering that agrees with those preferences.

paragraphs: This paper presents a compact circuit that reproduces temporal response and adaptation properties of the fly's photoreceptors and laminar layers. The circuit uses six transistors and two capacitors and operates in the subthreshold domain. A fabricated chip contains a 20-by-20 array of these pixels.

Adaptation to background intensity acts as gain control, allowing the circuit to maintain a strong response to transient changes. An external bias controls the adaptation time constant, meaning the timescale over which this adjustment occurs can be set. The design therefore combines sensitivity to change with an adjustable response to the prevailing light level.

Its temporal filtering also varies with illumination and signal-to-noise conditions. Across the reported range of 1 to 100 Hz, it behaves as a high-pass filter under bright light and as a low-pass filter under dim light, when signal-to-noise is low. This demonstrates a visual sensing circuit whose treatment of temporal changes adapts to the conditions under which it operates.
neurips-1997-silicon-retina-with-adaptiv.tldr: A compact silicon-retina circuit adapts its gain and temporal filtering to background illumination.

paragraphs: This paper brings stacking into unsupervised learning. Its task is multivariate density estimation: describing how probability is distributed across observations with multiple variables. Instead of choosing one density estimator, the method combines finite mixture models and kernel density estimators into a stacked estimate.

The key question is whether a learned combination can do better than selecting a single model or treating all models equally. The authors evaluate this on both simulated and real-world datasets. Their comparisons include selecting a model through cross-validation and combining models with uniform weights, two different ways to avoid learning a more tailored combination.

The reported stacked estimates outperform those alternatives and even the single best model selected using the independent test data. That last comparison is an intentionally advantaged model-selection reference. Within the reported experiments, it indicates that the benefit of combining estimators goes beyond merely identifying which individual candidate works best. The result extends stacking's usefulness from supervised prediction to estimating probability distributions.
neurips-1997-stacked-density-estimation-.tldr: Stacking density estimators outperforms individual-model selection and uniform averaging in the reported simulated and real-data experiments.

paragraphs: This paper examines how animals combine information from several cues when predicting rewards or punishments. Such predictions are studied through conditioning experiments and help explain how animals control their behavior. A standard account treats the prediction associated with each conditioned stimulus as a contribution to an overall sum.

The authors point to key experimental findings that this additive account cannot explain in some circumstances. They propose an alternative in which attention selects between the available stimuli. The central change concerns how multiple sources of predictive information are combined: their influence depends on selection rather than simply accumulating all individual predictions.

The resulting model takes the form of a mixture of experts and has a statistical foundation. It is also closely related to existing psychological proposals, connecting a formal modeling approach with ideas about attention in conditioning. Its significance lies in offering a principled alternative for the circumstances where additive predictions fail, with attentional selection built into the account of learning and behavior.
neurips-1997-statistical-models-of-condi.tldr: A statistically grounded mixture-of-experts model explains conditioning through attentional selection among cues.

paragraphs: This paper presents a neural-network model linking attention and auditory perception through synchronized oscillations between cortical areas. The broader architecture uses adaptive synchronization in the 5–15 Hz and 30–80 Hz ranges. Here the focus is rhythmic expectation and interaction between higher-order cortical processing and primary processing.

The model accounts for mismatch negativity in auditory event-related potentials and for psychological findings that the rhythmic structure of sounds affects how they separate into perceptual streams. Rhythm therefore plays a role in organizing what is heard, connecting the timing of incoming events with the attentional processes represented in the network.

Its timing mechanisms also explain how forming separate streams can lose information about the relative order of events across those streams. This connects successful grouping with a specific loss of timing information. The authors suggest that the model can reconcile the auditory-perception and attention theories of Jones and Bregman, providing a shared account of rhythmic organization, attention, and cross-stream temporal judgments.
neurips-1997-synchronized-auditory-and-c.tldr: A synchronized neural-network model links rhythmic expectation to auditory stream formation and the loss of timing information between streams.

paragraphs: This paper investigates natural gradient descent for training single-layer and multilayer perceptrons. The learning rule uses the inverse Fisher information matrix to determine its updates. Computing the information needed for those updates is therefore central to making the method practical for neural-network training.

The authors introduce a new representation of the Fisher information matrix for a stochastic multilayer perceptron. From that representation, they derive an algorithm for computing the natural gradient. The contribution links a mathematical description of the matrix to an explicit computational procedure, addressing the work required to carry out the learning rule.

When the input dimension is much larger than the number of hidden neurons, the algorithm has complexity linear in the input dimension. This condition is essential to the stated efficiency result. Simulations also support the efficiency and robustness of the learning rule. Together, the results provide a computational route to natural-gradient learning and empirical support for its behavior in the settings investigated.
neurips-1997-the-efficiency-and-the-robu.tldr: A new Fisher-matrix representation enables linear-complexity natural-gradient computation when input dimension greatly exceeds hidden-layer size.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the learning rate should decrease during online learning. Such an annealing schedule determines how update sizes change as learning proceeds. The authors focus on asymptotic dynamics, examining the behavior of the learning process in its long-run regime under different schedules.

They analyze the problem using two theoretical approaches: a master-equation approach and an order-parameter approach. They then examine how the results from the two descriptions relate to one another. This comparison connects two ways of studying the same learning dynamics, rather than treating their conclusions as unrelated prescriptions.

The analysis produces new results for optimal decay coefficients and how those coefficients depend on the number of hidden nodes in a two-layer architecture. The implication is that the best coefficient in a learning-rate decay schedule is tied to network structure in the studied setting. The contribution is a theoretical account of that dependence, grounded in a comparison of the two analytical methods.
neurips-1997-two-approaches-to-optimal-a.tldr: Two theoretical analyses connect optimal learning-rate decay coefficients to the number of hidden nodes in a two-layer network.

paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for discovering stochastic firing patterns in recordings from many neurons. The objective is to help describe information carried by populations acting in parallel. A model from the Helmholtz-machine family learns to predict observed spike patterns through a layer of hidden units.

Recorded spikes activate the observable layer, and ascending connections produce hidden-unit activity. That activity is then passed downward to predict the input pattern. The algorithm adds hidden units incrementally and adjusts their weights to improve the match between predictions and recordings, specifically by increasing a bound on the data's probability under the model.

This incremental strategy is greedy and does not guarantee a globally optimal solution, but the authors state that it is computationally tractable for large neuronal populations. They report benchmarks on artificial spike trains and promising early results from chronic multi-electrode cortical recordings. The work offers a practical route to learning population-level firing patterns while explicitly accepting a tradeoff in optimization.
neurips-1997-using-helmholtz-machines-to.tldr: An incrementally trained Helmholtz machine discovers neuronal firing patterns by learning to reconstruct multichannel spike recordings.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a randomized clustering method that works from pairwise similarities between data points. It uses a graph-based formulation and extends several deterministic approaches, including agglomerative clustering, minimum-cut methods, and connected components. The result is a common framework connecting methods that otherwise appear as separate clustering procedures.

The authors emphasize robustness to noise in the relationships between points. Accidental graph edges can connect groups that should remain separate, while small spurious clusters can distract from the larger organization of the data. The stochastic character of the proposed method is reported to make it more robust to these problems.

The demonstration uses a noisy example containing three spiraling bands, on which the authors report superior clustering. This example illustrates the method's handling of structured groups amid substantial noise. The contribution combines a unifying graph formulation with randomization intended to reduce sensitivity to misleading local relationships, and the supplied evidence supports that behavior through the stated spiral-band experiment.
neurips-1998-a-randomized-algorithm-for-.tldr: A randomized graph-based clustering framework improves robustness to accidental connections and small spurious clusters.

paragraphs: This paper develops tools for examining event-related brain responses one trial at a time. Averaging EEG trials improves signal-to-noise, but individual responses can differ substantially in timing and scalp distribution. The authors use independent component analysis to separate multichannel recordings into components with fixed spatial patterns and independent temporal activity.

Results from normal and autistic participants show separation of artifacts, stimulus-locked activity, response-locked activity, and background EEG. This allows artifacts to be removed from individual trials while retaining components associated with either the stimulus or the response. The decomposition makes different contributions to a recorded signal separately available for analysis.

The paper also introduces the ERP image, a two-dimensional visualization of individual trial responses. Sorting trials by reaction time reveals patterns in response timing and amplitude that relate to performance. Together, the analysis and visualization methods expose variability that averaging can obscure, offering tools for investigating both event-related components and their changing relationship to behavior across trials.
neurips-1998-analyzing-and-visualizing-s.tldr: ICA and ERP-image visualization separate EEG components and reveal behavior-linked variability across individual trials.

paragraphs: This paper develops a call-based system for detecting illegal use of mobile communication networks. Earlier approaches used features derived from individual users' calling patterns. The proposed approach instead organizes detection around a hierarchical regime-switching model, representing changing conditions through regimes whose probabilities must be inferred.

Fraud detection becomes a probabilistic inference problem: the system evaluates the probabilities of the regimes represented in the model. The authors perform that inference with the junction tree algorithm applied to the underlying graphical model. This gives the detection process a structured probabilistic basis rather than leaving the decision separate from the model of changing behavior.

The model's dynamics are learned from data using expectation-maximization, followed by discriminative training. The methods are assessed on fraud data from an actual mobile communication network. The contribution is an integrated detection approach that connects regime inference, learned temporal dynamics, and decision-focused training, with evaluation grounded in real network data rather than only an artificial setting.
neurips-1998-call-based-fraud-detection-.tldr: A hierarchical regime-switching model detects mobile-network fraud by inferring regime probabilities from call data.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how connection symmetry affects computation in recurrent neural networks. Symmetrically connected networks have been used to model many neural computations, but the authors emphasize a biological motivation for asymmetry: excitation and inhibition are separated in biological networks. That distinction raises the question of how well symmetric models capture relevant dynamics.

The authors compare asymmetric networks with their symmetric counterparts and show that their dynamical behavior can differ dramatically. The issue is therefore more than a change in how connections are represented. Altering symmetry can change the activity produced by the network as it evolves, with consequences for the computations that activity can support.

They also show how these differences can be used computationally, illustrating the results with a selective-amplifier network. The example connects the dynamical comparison to a concrete computational role. The contribution is an argument, supported by the studied networks, that asymmetry deserves attention as a source of computational behavior when modeling recurrent neural systems.
neurips-1998-computational-differences-b.tldr: Connection asymmetry produces major changes in recurrent-network dynamics that can be used for computation.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether the wake-sleep learning algorithm converges when used to train models with hidden variables. The algorithm is simple and can be applied to factor analysis, described here as a linear version of a Helmholtz machine. Yet its convergence had not been theoretically established even for that setting.

The authors develop a geometric interpretation of wake-sleep and compare it with the EM algorithm and the separately named em algorithm. This perspective provides a way to examine the behavior of the learning procedure and relate it to other methods for fitting models with hidden variables.

Using that analysis, they prove convergence for the factor-analysis model. They also give a condition for convergence in more general models. The distinction matters: the factor-analysis result is a convergence proof for a specific model, while the broader result identifies a condition under which convergence follows. The paper therefore adds theoretical support to a learning rule whose simplicity alone does not establish its behavior.
neurips-1998-convergence-of-the-wake-sle.tldr: A geometric analysis proves wake-sleep convergence for factor analysis and identifies a convergence condition for broader models.

paragraphs: This paper studies observations attached to pairs of objects drawn from two finite sets. Each observed pair contains one object from each set. This structure appears across language, information retrieval, preference analysis, and computer vision, motivating a learning framework organized around the paired nature of the data.

The authors propose a domain-independent approach based on statistical mixture models. It includes both flat and hierarchical latent-class structures, allowing the hidden organization used to explain observations to take different forms. The shared framework brings these alternatives together under the same general view of learning from pairs.

For model fitting, the paper introduces an annealed version of the standard expectation-maximization algorithm and evaluates it empirically on datasets from multiple domains. The contribution connects a common data structure, a family of latent-class models, and a corresponding fitting method. Its cross-domain evaluation reflects the central aim: to study dyadic observations through a reusable statistical framework rather than a separate formulation for every application.
neurips-1998-learning-from-dyadic-data-3.tldr: A mixture-model framework with annealed EM learns from paired-object observations across multiple application domains.

paragraphs: This paper applies TAP mean-field methods from statistical mechanics to Bayesian classification with Gaussian processes. The classification model places a Gaussian prior over a function that connects inputs to target probabilities. This provides a probabilistic description of possible predictive functions rather than specifying only one fitted function.

In the supplied formulation, the prior function has zero mean, and its second-order correlations determine its statistics. Those correlations describe how function values at different inputs are related. The mean-field approach is applied within this Gaussian-process classification setting, bringing a method developed for disordered physical systems into Bayesian learning.

A stated advantage over earlier approaches is that the method does not require knowledge of the distribution of inputs. This removes that particular information requirement from applying the approach. The authors provide simulation results on the Sonar dataset. The contribution is the adaptation of TAP methods to this classification problem, together with an empirical application and an explicit reduction in the assumptions about input distributions.
neurips-1998-mean-field-methods-for-clas.tldr: TAP mean-field methods are applied to Gaussian-process classification without requiring knowledge of the input distribution.

paragraphs: This paper modifies Q-learning to account for preferences about risk. Maximizing expected return can be inappropriate when a controller should avoid very bad outcomes or pursue high gains despite possible costs. The proposed method changes the optimality criterion through one continuous parameter, kappa, ranging from minus one to one.

At zero, the parameter recovers the usual expected-return objective. As it approaches one, the resulting solution becomes optimal for the worst case. Moving toward minus one makes the policy increasingly risk-seeking. The parameter therefore provides a single way to adjust the kind of outcome preference expressed by the learned policy.

The approach incorporates risk without transforming the cost model or enlarging the state space. The authors evaluate it by computing investment strategies in an artificial stock market. That application illustrates the intended role of the method: learning policies under different attitudes toward uncertain outcomes while retaining the original cost and state representation of the decision problem.
neurips-1998-risk-sensitive-reinforcemen.tldr: A modified Q-learning rule uses one parameter to move between expected-return optimization, worst-case protection, and risk-seeking behavior.
